newsitem.title: USA: Fed should target 1-3 pct inflation - IMF official.
newsitem.headline: Fed should target 1-3 pct inflation - IMF official.

text.p: The Federal Reserve should adopt an inflation target and set it at one to three percent, International Monetary Fund First Deputy Managing Director Stanley Fischer said on Tuesday.
"The Fed should operate with an explicit inflation target and it should be somewhere between one and three percent at present," Fischer told the National Economists Club.
Fischer, who emphasized that he was speaking on his own behalf and not for the IMF, said that inflation targets are becoming increasingly accepted around the world.

Fischer said that inflation targets clearly set out what a central bank should do. He also argued that the targets can be run in such a way as to allow central banks to take account of supply shocks -- such as oil price rise -- that increase inflation and reduce output.

He said the IMF believes that inflation targets are particularly useful for countries whose anti-inflation policies lack credibility. But the Fund thinks that such targets are not "evidently necessary" for countries that are performing well in containing inflation.
Fischer nevertheless argued for the adoption of an inflation target by the Fed.

While that has not been needed because of the success that Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan and his predecessor Paul Volcker have had in fighting inflation, there is no guarantee that their successors will be as competent, he said.
An inflation target would thus provide the Fed with an anchor in setting policy, he said.
Fischer said he put as much emphasis on maintaining the lower end of the proposed one-to-three percent target as on the upper end. Deflation has costs as well as inflation, he said.
He pointed to the difficulties that Japan -- which has had inflation of about zero -- has faced in reviving its economy over the last five years because it could only cut interest rates so far.

Fischer acknowledged though that such a change in Fed policy might not occur except in a crisis -- and there is not one now given the "remarkable" performance of U.S. monetary poilicy over the past decade.
